question: Carbon can form long chains because it exhibits ________ and shows ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**tetravalency; catenation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Carbon has the unique ability to form bonds with other atoms of carbon, giving rise to large molecules. This property is called **catenation**. These compounds may have **long chains** of carbon, **branched chains** of carbon, or even carbon atoms arranged in **rings**.
 
• The **carbon-carbon bond** is very **strong** and **stable**. This gives us a huge number of compounds with many carbon atoms linked to each other. This is primarily because the **size of the carbon atom** is very **small**, which enables the nucleus to hold on to the shared pairs of electrons strongly.
 
• Since carbon has a **valency of four**, it is capable of bonding with **four other atoms** of carbon or atoms of some other mono-valent element. This property is known as **tetravalency**.
 
• Carbon forms strong **covalent bonds** with **Oxygen**, **Hydrogen**, **Nitrogen**, and **Sulfur**, leading to compounds with specific properties that depend on the elements other than carbon present in the molecule.
 
• In the given question, the first blank refers to the number of bonds carbon can form, and the second refers to the property of self-linking. Therefore, carbon exhibits **tetravalency** and shows **catenation**. ***Hence, the statement regarding option B is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Allotropes of Carbon:**

 
 
• **Diamond**: In this, each carbon atom is bonded to **four other carbon atoms**, forming a rigid **three-dimensional structure**. It is the **hardest known natural substance** and has a very **high melting point**.
 
• **Graphite**: Each carbon atom is bonded to **three other carbon atoms** in the same plane giving a **hexagonal array**. It is a **good conductor of electricity** due to the presence of **free electrons**.
 
• **Fullerenes**: These form another class of carbon allotropes. The first one to be identified was **C-60**, which has carbon atoms arranged in the shape of a **football**. It was named **Buckminsterfullerene** after the American architect **Buckminster Fuller**.
 
 
 
• **Atomic Characteristics:**
 
 
• The **atomic number** of Carbon is **6**.
 
• The **electronic configuration** is **2, 4**, meaning it has **4 valence electrons** in its **L-shell**.
 
• Carbon belongs to **Group 14** and **Period 2** of the **Modern Periodic Table**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Silicon:**
 
 
• **Silicon** also belongs to **Group 14** and exhibits **catenation**. However, it forms compounds with hydrogen which have chains of up to **7 or 8 atoms** only. These compounds are **highly reactive** because the **Si-Si bond** is weaker than the **C-C bond**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Organic Chemistry:** The two characteristic features seen in carbon—**tetravalency** and **catenation**—put together give rise to a large number of compounds. Many have the same non-carbon atom or group of atoms attached to different carbon chains. These were initially called **organic compounds**.
 
• **Historical Context:** It was once thought that these organic compounds could only be formed within a living system through a **vital force** (proposed by **Berzelius**). However, this was disproved in **1828** when **Friedrich Wöhler** prepared **Urea** from **Ammonium cyanate**.
 
• **Isomerism:** Carbon compounds often show **structural isomerism**, where compounds have the same **molecular formula** but different **structural arrangements**. For example, **Butane** (**C4H10**) can exist as a straight chain (**n-butane**) or a branched chain (**isobutane**).
 
• **Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon:**
 
 
• **Saturated compounds** (Alkanes) contain only **single bonds** between carbon atoms and are generally **not very reactive**.
 
• **Unsaturated compounds** (Alkenes and Alkynes) contain **double** or **triple bonds** and are **more reactive** than saturated carbon compounds.
